The most important first step is to establish whether the twins share a placenta and/or an amniotic sac because this determines the risks and frequency of monitoring.”
“This is a viable twin pregnancy with two separate placental masses and a thick intertwin membrane demonstrating a lambda sign, consistent with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy.”
“This is a viable monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. There is a single shared placenta and a thin intertwin membrane with a T-sign. Both fetuses demonstrate cardiac activity.”

“This is a monochorionic monoamniotic twin pregnancy, with a single placenta and no visible dividing membrane. This pregnancy requires specialist management because of the increased risk of cord entanglement.”

Twin A has oligohydramnios with a poorly visualised bladder, while Twin B has significant polyhydramnios. These findings are concerning for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. I would urgently involve the fetal medicine team for staging and management.”

“There is significant intertwin growth discordance, with Twin A estimated at the 65th centile and Twin B below the 10th centile. items: “How would you manage a twin pregnancy?”

blocks.text: “I would first establish gestational age, chorionicity and amnionicity, because these determine the risk profile and surveillance schedule. I would assess the mother for anaemia, hypertension, diabetes and symptoms of preterm labour, and monitor fetal growth, amniotic fluid and wellbeing. In monochorionic twins I would specifically monitor for TTTS, TAPS and selective fetal growth restriction, while in monoamniotic twins I would be particularly concerned about cord entanglement. I would counsel the woman regarding prematurity, fetal growth problems, maternal complications and possible Caesarean or operative delivery. Finally, I would formulate an individualised delivery plan based on chorionicity, gestational age, fetal presentations, fetal wellbeing and local protocol.”
When you see TWINS in an OSCE, immediately think:
NUMBER → CHORIONICITY → AMNIONICITY → GROWTH → TTTS → PREMATURITY → DELIVERY
